newsitem.title: FRANCE: Franc seen stabilising at lower levels - dealers.
newsitem.headline: Franc seen stabilising at lower levels - dealers.

text.p: The franc weakened on Wednesday as investors began to take seriously the possibility of a win by the French left in Sunday's runoff parliamentary election, but dealers said they expected the damage to be limited.

They said that if the left wins the election and captures a majority in the National Assembly they expected the franc to establish a new range around 3.39 and 3.40 per mark, compared to its pre-election level around 3.36 per mark. If the right wins, the franc should bounce back, they said.
At 1600 GMT, the franc was at 3.3816 per mark, off its low of 3.3828 per mark touched earlier, which was its weakest point since February 4, when it reached 3.3839 per mark.
"My view is that the franc will continue to weaken a bit if the odds are perceived as higher for the left," said Philippe Brossard, economist with ABN Amro in Paris.
French markets, including the franc, never fully priced in a win by the left and are now having to adjust, said one currency dealer in Paris.
"People got too optimistic (about a centre-right win)," she said, adding that she expected the franc to stabilise over the next few days at around 3.3850 or 3.3900 per mark.
"The odds shifted this morning in the markets," Brossard said. "Until today the market thought there was a 50 percent chance the conservatives would win."

French bond and PIBOR futures also weakened on Wednesday, with June PIBOR dropping seven basis points to 96.23 and the June notionnnel contract dropping 28 ticks to 128.16. The Paris bourse lost 3.63 percent.
Other analysts said the franc sold off because of an accumulation of rumours sweeping through the market rather than any one report.
The most significant rumour was that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer would resign in protest against the German government's plan to revalue its gold reserves, they said.
The Bundesbank denied the resignation rumour. It was scheduled to issue a statement on asset issues at 1700 GMT.

"Tietmeyer resigning would suggest there's a big rift between the Bundesbank and the governemnt with respect to how they're going to get into EMU and that would make the markets worry that they won't see a single currency in 1999," said Steven Englander, economist with Smith Barney.
Wednesday also saw rumours that the Bank of France was intervening to support the franc and that private polls showed the left well-placed in the second round of voting.
The Bank of France declined to comment on the intervention rumours.
"As a general policy, we do not comment on rumours," a spokesman for the Bank said.

No trader contacted by Reuters confirmed that they had personally seen the Bank in the market. "I can neither confirm nor deny those rumours of intervention," said a trading desk head at a large French bank.
But dealers said the Bank seemed to be defending a level around 3.3820 francs per mark, after earlier trying to support it at 3.3775, dealers said.
The rumours about the poll were less significant, analysts said, because the Socialists are seen as unlikely to abandon France's commitment to launching a single currency in 1999.

"The polls that have suggested that the left would win are probably not too damaging to EMU in the short run since the french left has been very careful to say they support EMU," Smith Barney's Englander said.
